newsitem.title: UK: European grains jittery ahead of EU tender.
newsitem.headline: European grains jittery ahead of EU tender.

text.p: European grains markets were nervous ahead of Thursday's final EU export tender of the year, traders said.
But export hopes helped bolster prices.

French wheat was firmer on the week despite reaffirmation of his warning of a slowing in EU exports by Guy Legras, the European Commission's director general for agriculture. Short -term loading requirements helped underpin prices, dealers said.
French prices were also lifted by firmer world prices and fresh export propects.
Following Legras' remarks, nervous exporters are awaiting Thursday's EU grain auction, the last for 1996, to get clues over the Commission's export plans.
Short-term loading requirements and expectations that the world largest barley importer, Saudi Arabia, may soon shop again for barley, helped support barley prices.
Maize prices were steady to slightly firmer ahead of the EU's decision on gene maize sales.
Dealers said the decision to clear the sale of gene-altered maize would have a bearish impact on domestic maize prices.
Seasonal lethargy has set in in the UK, but the volatility of sterling is keeping the market nervous, traders said.
A shortage of sellers remains the main problem for UK wheat. People want to buy it. "The market is very well bid. There's a lot of buying interest for wheat," one trader said.

Sterling is up this morning, but the reaction is not what traders normally expect. "Normally the rise would have taken a pound off and sellers would be looking for homes," the trader said. But this year sellers were staying away whenever prices turned down.
Others confirmed that they had seen farm selling over the past week, but only on days when the market had turned up.

Even though the recent market strength has eroded the competitive position of UK grain against French, UK traders remain optimistic on exports. UK wheat's price advantage has been as low as $4 this week, having been up to $10 earlier in the season, one said.
Spanish dealers said trade was thin ahead of the Christmas period and prices were largely static.
Ex-farm feed and durum wheat prices remained unchanged. Dealers said the durum wheat market had almost entirely dried up, with very limited supply and demand.
Milling wheat prices rose 600 pesetas across the board, with demand mainly coming from the south but supply only available in the north and middle of the country.
Barley and maize prices held steady although trade was flat.
The traders said the maize market was still nervous ahead of the European Commission decision on whether it will allow countries to import U.S. gene-modified maize.
Dealers said they did not expect trade in grains to pick up until the second week of January.
Dealers on Italian cereal markets have been mostly buying for January delivery as the market gets ready to shut down for the Christmas holiday season.
German wheat sales were seasonally slow but sellers were keeping up prices ahead of the new year, brokers said.
"Nominal prices are even a touch higher here or there because sellers need to account for storage costs," one said.
"But I believe there won't be any more sales this year as old business is being carried out and some ships have failed to arrive...this will keep us occupied well into early January."
Prices were underpinned by higher UK and French levels.
But early 1997 prices had little upside potential because of feed wheat supply pressure from a number of western European origins, brokers said.
Sellers pointed to possible farmer retention if levels were to fall, and latent Polish and Uzbek wheat demand.
German barley markets took support from some sales to the Netherlands and renewed seller assertiveness after feed grain supply pressure had weighed on post-harvest markets.
